claim: Recovery from serious neurological injury requires substantial rewiring of neural circuits.
source: Recovery from serious neurological injury requires substantial rewiring of neural circuits.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific understanding about neurological recovery.

claim: Precisely-timed electrical stimulation could be used to restore corrective feedback mechanisms and promote adaptive plasticity after neurological insult, such as spinal cord injury (SCI) or stroke.
source: Precisely-timed electrical stimulation could be used to restore corrective feedback mechanisms and promote adaptive plasticity after neurological insult, such as spinal cord injury (SCI) or stroke.
evidence: This is a hypothesis statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that closed-loop vagus nerve stimulation (CLV) based on the synaptic eligibility trace leads to dramatic recovery from the most common forms of SCI.
source: This study provides the first evidence that closed-loop vagus nerve stimulation (CLV) based on the synaptic eligibility trace leads to dramatic recovery from the most common forms of SCI.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing improved recovery with CLV in both unilateral and bilateral SCI models.

claim: The addition of CLV to rehabilitation promoted substantially more recovery of forelimb function compared to rehabilitation alone following chronic unilateral or bilateral cervical SCI in a rat model.
source: The addition of CLV to rehabilitation promoted substantially more recovery of forelimb function compared to rehabilitation alone following chronic unilateral or bilateral cervical SCI in a rat model.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the behavioral data shown in Figures 1c, 2a, and 4a comparing CLV groups to rehabilitation alone.

claim: Triggering stimulation on the most successful movements is critical to maximize recovery.
source: Triggering stimulation on the most successful movements is critical to maximize recovery.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison between Top 20% CLV and Bottom 20% CLV groups shown in Figure 1c, where timing of stimulation with successful movements was critical.

claim: CLV enhances recovery by strengthening synaptic connectivity from remaining motor networks to the grasping muscles in the forelimb.
source: CLV enhances recovery by strengthening synaptic connectivity from remaining motor networks to the grasping muscles in the forelimb.
evidence: This is supported by the retrograde transneuronal tracing data shown in Figures 2d and 4d demonstrating increased labeled neurons in motor networks.

claim: The benefits of CLV persist long after the end of stimulation because connectivity in critical neural circuits has been restored.
source: The benefits of CLV persist long after the end of stimulation because connectivity in critical neural circuits has been restored.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing maintained recovery after cessation of stimulation (Figures 1c, 2a, 4a) and anatomical data showing increased synaptic connectivity (Figures 2d, 4d).

claim: Many methods have been developed to enhance synaptic plasticity in hopes of enhancing recovery.
source: Many methods have been developed to enhance synaptic plasticity in hopes of enhancing recovery.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field that reflects established knowledge.

claim: These methods have largely failed in the clinic likely due to the challenge of precisely targeting specific synapses and absence of testing in clinically-relevant models (Gladstone et al., 2006; Levy et al., 2016).
source: Unfortunately, these methods have largely failed in the clinic likely due to the challenge of precisely targeting specific synapses and absence of testing in clinically-relevant models (Gladstone et al., 2006; Levy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Real-time control of neural activity provides a new avenue to promote synaptic plasticity in specific networks and restore function after injury (Engineer et al., 2011; Nishimura et al., 2013; McPherson et al., 2015; Guggenmos et al., 2013).
source: Real-time control of neural activity provides a new avenue to promote synaptic plasticity in specific networks and restore function after injury (Engineer et al., 2011; Nishimura et al., 2013; McPherson et al., 2015; Guggenmos et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human and animal studies demonstrate that precisely timed vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) can improve recovery of sensory and motor function.
source: Human and animal studies demonstrate that precisely timed vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) can improve recovery of sensory and motor function.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the literature citations that follow in the manuscript.

claim: VNS engages neuromodulatory networks and triggers release of pro-plasticity factors including norepinephrine, acetylcholine, serotonin, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and fibroblast growth factor (Hays, 2016; Hulsey et al., 2017; Hulsey et al., 2016).
source: VNS engages neuromodulatory networks and triggers release of pro-plasticity factors including norepinephrine, acetylcholine, serotonin, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and fibroblast growth factor (Hays, 2016; Hulsey et al., 2017; Hulsey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VNS influences expression and phosphorylation of proteins associated with structural and synaptic plasticity, including Arc, CaMKII, TrkB, and glutamate receptors (Alvarez-Dieppa et al., 2016; Furmaga et al., 2012).
source: This in turn influences expression and phosphorylation of proteins associated with structural and synaptic plasticity, including Arc, CaMKII, TrkB, and glutamate receptors (Alvarez-Dieppa et al., 2016; Furmaga et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Engagement of neuromodulatory networks activates a transient synaptic eligibility trace to support spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) (He et al., 2015).
source: Engagement of neuromodulatory networks activates a transient synaptic eligibility trace to support spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) (He et al., 2015), thus raising the prospect that closed-loop neuromodulatory strategies may provide a means to direct specific, long-lasting plasticity to enhance recovery after neurological injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Repeatedly pairing sensory or motor events with brief bursts of VNS yields robust plasticity in sensory or motor cortex that is specific to the paired experience (Engineer et al., 2011; Hulsey et al., 2016).
source: Indeed, in the absence of neurological damage, repeatedly pairing sensory or motor events with brief bursts of VNS yields robust plasticity in sensory or motor cortex that is specific to the paired experience (Engineer et al., 2011; Hulsey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The addition of VNS to rehabilitative training improves recovery in rodent models of unilateral brain injury and in chronic stroke patients (Hays, 2016; Khodaparast et al., 2016; Pruitt et al., 2016; Hays et al., 2014a; Dawson et al., 2016).
source: Moreover, the addition of VNS to rehabilitative training improves recovery in rodent models of unilateral brain injury and in chronic stroke patients, highlighting the clinical potential of closed-loop neuromodulatory strategies (Hays, 2016; Khodaparast et al., 2016; Pruitt et al., 2016; Hays et al., 2014a; Dawson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SCI resulted in a 77% reduction in volitional forelimb strength, consistent with paresis observed in many cervical SCI patients.
source: SCI resulted in a 77% reduction in volitional forelimb strength, consistent with paresis observed in many cervical SCI patients (Figure 1c, PRE v. Wk 8, Paired t-test, t(29) = 37.34, p=4.4×10−26, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing pre-injury to post-injury performance.

claim: Top 20% CLV substantially boosted recovery of volitional forelimb strength compared to equivalent rehabilitative training without CLV (Rehab alone).
source: Top 20% CLV substantially boosted recovery of volitional forelimb strength compared to equivalent rehabilitative training without CLV (Rehab alone), demonstrating that CLV enhances recovery of motor function after SCI (Figure 1c; Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, Interaction; F[6,120]=3.88, p=1.43×10−3; Videos 3–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing Top 20% CLV to Rehab alone.

claim: CLV resulted in lasting recovery after the cessation of stimulation after week 11.
source: CLV resulted in lasting recovery after the cessation of stimulation after week 11, consistent with the notion that CLV restores function in critical motor networks (Top 20% CLV; Wk 11 v. Wk 12; Paired t-test, t(12) = −0.89, p=0.38).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference in performance between week 11 (with stimulation) and week 12 (without stimulation).

claim: Bottom 20% CLV failed to improve forelimb strength compared to Rehab alone.
source: Despite equivalent rehabilitation and a comparable number of stimulations delivered during task performance (Figure 1d,e), Bottom 20% CLV resulted in substantially diminished recovery compared to Top 20% CLV (Figure 1c, Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, Interaction; F[6,114]=2.40, p=0.03, Video 5) and failed to improve forelimb strength compared to Rehab alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 1c comparing Bottom 20% CLV to Rehab alone.

claim: Closed-loop neuromodulation paired with the most successful movements during rehabilitation improves recovery of motor function after cervical SCI.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that closed-loop neuromodulation paired with the most successful movements during rehabilitation improves recovery of motor function after cervical SCI.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the behavioral data comparing different CLV timing paradigms.

claim: CLV delivered within 2 s of successful trials increases recovery, whereas CLV separated 25 s from successful trials fails to yield substantial benefits.
source: CLV delivered within 2 s of successful trials increases recovery, whereas CLV separated 25 s from successful trials fails to yield substantial benefits.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1f comparing Delayed Top 20% CLV to Bottom 20% CLV.

claim: The temporal precision limit for CLV is near 10 s, consistent with the synaptic eligibility trace hypothesis (He et al., 2015).
source: These findings support a temporal precision limit for CLV near 10 s, consistent with the synaptic eligibility trace hypothesis (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the timing data and supported by citation to the synaptic eligibility trace theory.

claim: Top 50% CLV substantially improved recovery of forelimb function compared to Rehab alone.
source: Top 50% CLV substantially improved recovery of forelimb function compared to Rehab alone, which provides an independent confirmation that CLV enhances recovery after SCI (Figure 2a, Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, Interaction; F[6,174]=3.56, p=2.38×10−3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing Top 50% CLV to Rehab alone.

claim: The rate and degree of recovery were comparable in the Top 50% CLV and the Top 20% CLV groups.
source: The rate and degree of recovery were comparable in the Top 50% CLV and the Top 20% CLV groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that timing is more important than quantity of stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Timing is more important than quantity of stimulation for CLV-mediated recovery.
source: The rate and degree of recovery were comparable in the Top 50% CLV and the Top 20% CLV groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that timing is more important than quantity of stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between Top 20% and Top 50% CLV groups showing similar outcomes despite different amounts of stimulation.

claim: Unilateral SCI caused substantial damage to gray matter, rubrospinal, and propriospinal tracts in the right hemicord, while largely sparing the right corticospinal tract and the entirety of the left hemicord.
source: Unilateral SCI caused substantial damage to gray matter, rubrospinal, and propriospinal tracts in the right hemicord, while largely sparing the right corticospinal tract and the entirety of the left hemicord.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: CLV resulted in eight times more motor cortex sites that generated grasp movements in the impaired forelimb compared to Rehab alone.
source: CLV resulted in eight times more motor cortex sites that generated grasp movements in the impaired forelimb compared to Rehab alone (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Unpaired t-test, t(10) = 2.28, p=0.04), providing the first evidence that CLV induces large-scale plasticity in corticospinal networks after neurological injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by ICMS mapping data comparing Top 50% CLV to Rehab alone.

claim: CLV induces large-scale plasticity in corticospinal networks after neurological injury.
source: CLV resulted in eight times more motor cortex sites that generated grasp movements in the impaired forelimb compared to Rehab alone (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Unpaired t-test, t(10) = 2.28, p=0.04), providing the first evidence that CLV induces large-scale plasticity in corticospinal networks after neurological injury.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the ICMS mapping data.

claim: CLV resulted in a five-fold increase in labeled neurons in motor cortex compared to Rehab alone.
source: CLV resulted in a five-fold increase in labeled neurons in motor cortex compared to Rehab alone (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Unpaired t-test, t(9) = 7.63, p=3.2×10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde transneuronal tracing data using PRV-152.

claim: The magnitude of the increase in synaptic connectivity is comparable to the seven-fold increase in the number of motor cortex sites that produce grasp.
source: The magnitude of this increase in synaptic connectivity is comparable to the seven-fold increase in the number of motor cortex sites that produce grasp.
evidence: This is a comparison between the anatomical tracing data and the ICMS mapping data.

claim: CLV failed to increase neuronal labeling of spinal motor neurons, red nucleus neurons or propriospinal neurons after unilateral SCI.
source: CLV failed to increase neuronal labeling of spinal motor neurons, red nucleus neurons or propriospinal neurons (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the retrograde transneuronal tracing data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: CLV did not influence lesion extent after unilateral SCI.
source: Additionally, CLV did not influence lesion extent (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of lesion size.

claim: Anatomical plasticity in the spared corticospinal network contributes to enhanced recovery when CLV is added to rehabilitative training after unilateral SCI.
source: Together, these results are consistent with anatomical plasticity in the spared corticospinal network contributing to enhanced recovery when CLV is added to rehabilitative training after SCI (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined ICMS, tracing, and behavioral data after unilateral SCI.

claim: CLV may prove ineffective if the CST is destroyed.
source: The observation that CLV improves recovery and enhances functional and anatomical plasticity in corticospinal networks suggests that CLV may prove ineffective if the CST is destroyed.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that CLV enhanced corticospinal plasticity after unilateral SCI.

claim: Bilateral injury virtually eliminates the CST on both sides of the cord.
source: We therefore evaluated motor recovery in a bilateral injury model that virtually eliminates the CST on both sides of the cord (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Despite profound damage from bilateral SCI, CLV more than doubled the degree of forelimb motor recovery compared to Rehab alone.
source: Despite profound damage, CLV more than doubled the degree of forelimb motor recovery compared to Rehab alone (Figure 4a, Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, Interaction; F[6,144]=5.29, p=7.62×10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data after bilateral SCI.

claim: CLV could be clinically useful after bilateral SCI.
source: The observation that CLV can improve recovery following bilateral SCI suggests CLV could be clinically useful.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effectiveness of CLV in the bilateral SCI model.

claim: CLV enhances recovery after bilateral SCI by promoting plasticity in the rubrospinal and propriospinal pathways.
source: We hypothesized that CLV enhances recovery by promoting plasticity in the rubrospinal and propriospinal pathways, which were damaged, but not eliminated, by this injury (Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by the anatomical tracing data showing increased labeling in these pathways.

claim: CLV doubled the number of labeled red nucleus neurons and C3/4 propriospinal neurons compared to Rehab alone after bilateral SCI.
source: Indeed, CLV doubled the number of labeled red nucleus neurons and C3/4 propriospinal neurons compared to Rehab alone (Figure 3d and Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Unpaired t-test, Red Nucleus: t(4) = 3.89, p=0.018; Propriospinal: t(4) = 2.77, p=0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde transneuronal tracing data after bilateral SCI.

claim: CLV had no effect on reorganization of motor cortex after bilateral SCI.
source: Consistent with the extensive damage to the corticospinal pathway, CLV had no effect on reorganization of motor cortex (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Unpaired t-test, t(12) = −0.13, p=0.90)
evidence: This claim is supported by ICMS mapping data after bilateral SCI.

claim: CLV failed to increase the number of labeled neurons in the motor cortex after bilateral SCI.
source: Consistent with the extensive damage to the corticospinal pathway, CLV had no effect on reorganization of motor cortex (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Unpaired t-test, t(12) = −0.13, p=0.90) and failed to increase the number of labeled neurons in the motor cortex (Figure 3d, Unpaired t-test, t(4) = 0.83, p=0.45).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde transneuronal tracing data after bilateral SCI.

claim: CLV is capable of supporting recovery following SCI by strengthening anatomical connectivity within remaining pathways.
source: These results suggest that CLV is capable of supporting recovery following SCI by strengthening anatomical connectivity within remaining pathways (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the combined data from both unilateral and bilateral SCI models.

claim: A novel closed-loop neuromodulation strategy was developed to make use of the high temporal precision of the synaptic eligibility trace.
source: In this study, we developed a novel closed-loop neuromodulation strategy to make use of the high temporal precision of the synaptic eligibility trace.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach developed in the study.

claim: Activation of the vagus nerve improves recovery when reliably delivered within seconds of a successful movement.
source: We demonstrate that activation of the vagus nerve improves recovery when reliably delivered within seconds of a successful movement
evidence: This claim is supported by the timing experiments shown in Figure 1f.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that CLV enhances reorganization of synaptic connectivity in remaining networks in two non-overlapping models of SCI.
source: we provide the first evidence that CLV enhances reorganization of synaptic connectivity in remaining networks in two non-overlapping models of SCI.
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical tracing data from both unilateral and bilateral SCI models.

claim: The flexibility to promote reorganization in a range of pathways is a critical benefit of CLV, given the great heterogeneity in the etiology, location, and extent of damage present in SCI patients.
source: The flexibility to promote reorganization in a range of pathways is a critical benefit of CLV, given the great heterogeneity in the etiology, location, and extent of damage present in SCI patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CLV enhanced different pathways depending on which were spared.

claim: Classical studies by Skinner demonstrate that adaptive reinforcement of successive approximations, or shaping, drives behavior toward a desired response (Skinner, 1953).
source: Classical studies by Skinner demonstrate that adaptive reinforcement of successive approximations, or shaping, drives behavior toward a desired response (Skinner, 1953).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to classical behavioral psychology literature.

claim: The principle of shaping has been adopted for use in rehabilitation, with the intention to reinforce successively better movements (Wood, 1990).
source: This principle has been adopted for use in rehabilitation, with the intention to reinforce successively better movements (Wood, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to rehabilitation literature.

claim: Enhanced recovery was observed only when CLV was paired with trials that approximated the desired outcome.
source: Enhanced recovery was observed only when CLV was paired with trials that approximated the desired outcome, highlight the importance of timing for closed-loop stimulation to shape behavioral outcomes and maximize recovery.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison between Top 20% CLV and Bottom 20% CLV groups.

claim: The magnitude of neuromodulatory activation elicited by an event is directly proportional to the surprise, or unpredictability, of the event (Hangya et al., 2015; Hollerman and Schultz, 1998; Sara and Segal, 1991).
source: The magnitude of neuromodulatory activation elicited by an event is directly proportional to the surprise, or unpredictability, of the event (Hangya et al., 2015; Hollerman and Schultz, 1998; Sara and Segal, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroscience literature on reward prediction.

claim: This phenomenon is ascribed to reward prediction error (Schultz, 2002).
source: This phenomenon is ascribed to reward prediction error (Schultz, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to reward prediction error literature.

claim: Unsurprising events fail to activate neuromodulatory systems, and even rewarding events fail to trigger neuromodulator release if they are expected.
source: Unsurprising events fail to activate neuromodulatory systems, and even rewarding events fail to trigger neuromodulator release if they are expected.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about reward prediction error.

claim: The predictability and accompanying tedium of long, frustrating rehabilitation and the minimal reinforcement of practicing a previously simple motor task blunts plasticity and limits recovery after SCI.
source: We posit the predictability and accompanying tedium of long, frustrating rehabilitation and the minimal reinforcement of practicing a previously simple motor task blunts plasticity and limits recovery after SCI.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reward prediction error theory applied to rehabilitation.

claim: The closed-loop neuromodulation strategy circumvents the limitations of rehabilitation by artificially engaging neuromodulatory networks and providing a repeated, non-adapting reinforcing signal typically associated with surprising consequences (Hays, 2016; Hulsey et al., 2017; Hulsey et al., 2016).
source: The closed-loop neuromodulation strategy developed here circumvents this by artificially engaging neuromodulatory networks and providing a repeated, non-adapting reinforcing signal typically associated with surprising consequences (Hays, 2016; Hulsey et al., 2017; Hulsey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism supported by citations and the experimental results.

claim: CLV drives temporally-precise neuromodulatory release to convert the synaptic eligibility trace in neuronal networks that generate optimal motor control to long-lasting plasticity (He et al., 2015).
source: CLV drives temporally-precise neuromodulatory release to convert the synaptic eligibility trace in neuronal networks that generate optimal motor control to long-lasting plasticity (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citation and the experimental results showing lasting plasticity.

claim: CLV is a minimally-invasive, safe strategy to provide precisely-timed engagement of multiple neuromodulatory networks to boost plasticity during rehabilitation (Hays, 2016).
source: CLV is a minimally-invasive, safe strategy to provide precisely-timed engagement of multiple neuromodulatory networks to boost plasticity during rehabilitation (Hays, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and the safety profile observed in the study.

claim: Preliminary results in chronic stroke and tinnitus patients highlight the clinical potential of CLV, while delivering less than 1% of the total FDA-approved amount of stimulation (Dawson et al., 2016; De Ridder et al., 2014; Ben-Menachem, 2001).
source: Preliminary results in chronic stroke and tinnitus patients highlight the clinical potential of CLV, while delivering less than 1% of the total FDA-approved amount of stimulation (Dawson et al., 2016; De Ridder et al., 2014; Ben-Menachem, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The flexibility to deliver stimulation with a variety of rehabilitative exercises raises the possibility to design CLV-based therapies to target motor dysfunction of the lower limbs, somatosensory loss, and bowel and bladder issues, all of which are prevalent in SCI patients.
source: Moreover, the flexibility to deliver stimulation with a variety of rehabilitative exercises raises the possibility to design CLV-based to target motor dysfunction of the lower limbs, somatosensory loss, and bowel and bladder issues, all of which are prevalent in SCI patients.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications based on the current results.

claim: Delineation of the timing requirements and documentation of neuronal changes driven by CLV in this study provide a framework for development of this strategy for a range of neurological conditions, including stroke, peripheral nerve injury, and post-traumatic stress disorder (Hays, 2016; Lozano, 2011).
source: Delineation of the timing requirements and documentation of neuronal changes driven by CLV in this study provide a framework for development of this strategy for a range of neurological conditions, including stroke, peripheral nerve injury, and post-traumatic stress disorder (Hays, 2016; Lozano, 2011).
evidence: This is a summary claim about the broader implications of the study, supported by the data and citations.

claim: Adult female Sprague Dawley rats (N = 181) were used in this study.
source: Adult female Sprague Dawley rats (N = 181) used in this study were housed one per cage (12 hr light/dark cycle).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental subjects.

claim: Rats were trained to proficiency on the isometric pull task.
source: One hundred and sixty-nine rats were trained to proficiency on the isometric pull task as in our previous studies (Khodaparast et al., 2016; Pruitt et al., 2016; Hays et al., 2013; Sloan et al., 2015; Hays et al., 2014b; Hays et al., 2016; Khodaparast et al., 2013; Pruitt et al., 2014; Meyers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citations to previous studies using the same methods.

claim: After reaching task proficiency, rats received a unilateral contusive injury (N = 128) or bilateral contusive injury (N = 41) of the cervical spinal cord.
source: After reaching task proficiency (85% success rate on ten consecutive sessions), rats received a unilateral contusive injury (N = 128) or bilateral contusive injury (N = 41) of the cervical spinal cord.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental procedures.

claim: Eighty-seven rats were excluded from the study due to mortality (N = 20), inability to perform the task after injury (N = 25), or VNS device failure (N = 42).
source: Eighty-seven rats were excluded from the study due to mortality (N = 20), inability to perform the task after injury (N = 25), or VNS device failure (N = 42).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about subject exclusion criteria.

claim: Bilateral SCI rats were given two additional weeks of recovery time due to their larger spinal lesion and slower return to recumbency.
source: Bilateral SCI rats were given two additional weeks of recovery time due to their larger spinal lesion and slower return to recumbency (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: The isometric pull task is a fully automated and quantitative assay to measure multiple parameters of forelimb force generation.
source: The isometric pull task is a fully automated and quantitative assay to measure multiple parameters of forelimb force generation and was performed similar to previous descriptions (Khodaparast et al., 2016; Pruitt et al., 2016; Hays et al., 2013; Sloan et al., 2015; Hays et al., 2014b, 2016; Khodaparast et al., 2013; Pruitt et al., 2014; Meyers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Experimenters were blind to treatment group at all times throughout behavioral testing.
source: Experimenters were blind to treatment group at all times throughout behavioral testing.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about experimental blinding.

claim: The reward threshold was scaled adaptively based on the median peak force of the 10 preceding trials, with a fixed bounded minimum of 10 grams and maximum of 120 g.
source: The reward threshold was scaled adaptively based on the median peak force of the 10 preceding trials, with a fixed bounded minimum of 10 grams and maximum of 120 g based on previous studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Ganzer et al., 2016a; Meyers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the behavioral task supported by citations.

claim: Rats were trained until they reached proficiency, defined as 10 consecutive sessions in which greater than 85% of trials exceeded 120 g.
source: Rats were trained until they reached proficiency, defined as a 10 consecutive sessions in which greater than 85% of trials exceeded 120 g.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the training criterion.

claim: For unilateral SCI, the right spinal hemicord was contused using the Infinite Horizon Impact Device with a force of 200 kilodynes and zero dwell time.
source: For unilateral SCI, the right spinal hemicord was contused using the Infinite Horizon Impact Device with a force of 200 kilodynes and zero dwell time as previously reported (Precision Systems and Instrumentation, Lexington, KY; impactor tip diameter = 1.25 mm) (Ganzer et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the injury procedure supported by citation.

claim: For bilateral SCI rats, the midline of the spinal cord was contused with a force of 225 kilodynes and zero dwell time (impactor tip diameter = 2.5 mm).
source: For bilateral SCI rats, the midline of the spinal cord was contused with a force of 225 kilodynes and zero dwell time (impactor tip diameter = 2.5 mm).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the bilateral injury procedure.

claim: After bilateral SCI, rats took significantly longer to return to recumbency and forepaw plantar placement compared to unilateral SCI rats.
source: After bilateral SCI, rats took significantly longer to return to recumbency and forepaw plantar placement compared to unilateral SCI rats (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: Stimulation of the left cervical branch of the vagus nerve was performed using low current levels to avoid cardiac effects (Engineer et al., 2011).
source: Stimulation of the left cervical branch of the vagus nerve was performed using low current levels to avoid cardiac effects (Engineer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citation.

claim: Animals that failed to demonstrate a reliable drop in oxygen saturation at the end of therapy were excluded.
source: Animals that failed to demonstrate a reliable drop in oxygen saturation at the end of therapy were excluded.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about exclusion criteria.

claim: Each stimulation train consisted of 16 × 100 µsec 0.8 mA biphasic pulses delivered at 30 Hz.
source: Each stimulation train consisted of 16 × 100 µsec 0.8 mA biphasic pulses delivered at 30 Hz.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the stimulation parameters.

claim: No groups received VNS on the final week of rehabilitative training to assess effects lasting after the cessation of stimulation.
source: No groups received VNS on the final week of rehabilitative training (Week 12 for unilateral and Week 14 for bilateral SCI) to assess effects lasting after the cessation of stimulation.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental design.

claim: These VNS parameters do not cause discomfort and do not alter reaching behavior (Hulsey et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2012).
source: These parameters do not cause discomfort and do not alter reaching behavior (Hulsey et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Terminal intracortical microstimulation mapping (ICMS) of motor cortex was performed in a subset of unilateral SCI (Rehab alone, N = 6; Top 50% CLV, N = 6) and bilateral SCI (Rehab alone, N = 7; Top 50% CLV, N = 7) rats at the end of therapy.
source: Terminal intracortical microstimulation mapping (ICMS) of motor cortex was performed in a subset of unilateral SCI (Rehab alone, N = 6; Top 50% CLV, N = 6) and bilateral SCI (Rehab alone, N = 7; Top 50% CLV, N = 7) rats at the end of therapy.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the ICMS experiments.

claim: Mapping experiments were performed blinded with two experimenters.
source: Mapping experiments were performed blinded with two experimenters similar to previous studies (Hulsey et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about experimental blinding supported by citations.

claim: Transsynaptic tracer injections using pseudorabies virus 152 (PRV-152) were performed in a subset of unilateral SCI (Rehab, n = 6; VNS + Rehab, n = 5) and bilateral SCI (Rehab, n = 3; VNS + Rehab, n = 3) rats following the respective end of therapy.
source: Transsynaptic tracer injections using pseudorabies virus 152 (PRV-152) were performed in a subset of unilateral SCI (Rehab, n = 6; VNS + Rehab, n = 5) and bilateral SCI (Rehab, n = 3; VNS + Rehab, n = 3) rats following the respective end of therapy.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the tracing experiments.

claim: 15 µL of PRV-152 (~8.06 ± 0.49 x 10^8 plaque-forming units) was injected into the belly of each muscle across three separate sites.
source: 15 µL of PRV-152 (~8.06 ± 0.49 x 108 plaque-forming units) was injected into the belly of each muscle across three separate sites.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the viral injection procedure.

claim: At 6–6.5 days post-infection, consistent layer five cortical labeling was observed across injured or uninjured animals.
